title: The thread that won't break
hookLine: such a thread doesn't break, burn, get dirty or wear out (Asa di Var, ang 471)

cards: Open any drawer at home and you'll find something that wore out. A sweater with elbows gone thin. A phone cable split near the plug.
A favorite shirt washed one too many times. Everything made of fiber frays eventually. Cotton breaks under strain.
It burns in a second near a flame. It picks up stains. And even protected from all that, time thins it out.
Guru Nanak named all four ways a thread can fail, one by one, about the thread of compassion from yesterday.

teach.h: IT WON'T BREAK, STAIN, BURN, OR BE LOST.
teach.b: Here's how the salok on ang 471 continues, in paraphrase. Such a thread doesn't break. It doesn't get dirty.
It doesn't burn. It isn't lost. Blessed, Nanak says, are the people who go about wearing it around their necks.
Four nots. One way to hear them: breaking is strain, the hard week, the argument, the shock. Dirt is the slow grime of daily life: resentment, envy, gossip.
Burning is the sudden fire: rage, disaster, loss. And being lost is time itself, the way things simply slip away. A cotton thread can't survive any of these for long.
A thread spun from compassion, contentment, restraint and truth, the salok says, survives all four.
Then Guru Nanak looks at the outer thread with plain eyes. It's bought for a few coins, he says, and put on in a ceremony. When the body dies, it falls away; the person leaves without it.
Whatever is tied to the body goes the way of the body. The next salok in the var adds an answer.

Through trust in the Name, honor arises, and praise of the One is the true thread. Worn that way, it doesn't break in the Court of the Lord. Sikh teaching reads this as a question about what goes with us.
Not possessions, not status, not even the symbols we're given.

teach.h: WHAT GOES IS WHAT WE'VE BECOME.
teach.b: What goes is what we've become.
A grandmother who has worn that thread for decades, patient at the stove, honest at the market, takes it with her. The cotton one stays behind.

how: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching holds that virtues and the praise of the One are what go with a person beyond death.

games.q: the thread that lasts — tap the pairs.
p: the slow grime of envy and gossip
falls away when the body dies

s: the salok says the thread of the soul is lost when the body dies
the outer thread falls away; the thread of the soul isn't lost.
the salok names four things the thread of the soul survives
it doesn't break, get dirty, burn, or get lost.
the next salok calls praise of the One the true thread
worn that way, it doesn't break in the Lord's Court.

games.q: you're holding two threads: one cotton, one spun from compassion and truth. after a lifetime, which one is still with you?
o: the cotton one, if you're careful.
the one of compassion and truth.
games.why: the outer thread falls away when the body dies. the thread of the soul doesn't break, burn, get dirty or get lost.

practice: Picture yourself many years from now, most of today's worries long gone, and ask what in you will still be there: not a job title, maybe a way of listening, a patience, a love for certain people.
Let one quality come forward, and picture it as a thread, already strong, getting stronger. If you pray, say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Compassion, one strand of the soul's thread: in Guru Nanak's salok, spun with contentment, restraint and truth, it doesn't break, get dirty, burn, or get lost, and it goes with you.

carryVoice: Your line: it won't wear out. What goes with us is what we've become. Five hundred fifty-five days now.
